concepts.one_liner: Parametric texture models represent a texture image using a small vector of parameters, typically around 1,000 dimensions.

concepts.title: Nonparametric Texture Models

position.section_title: Efros-Leung Texture Analysis and Synthesis Model

concepts.one_liner: Nonparametric texture models are a class of image models that became dominant after 2000, preceding the emergence of neural generative models.
concepts.content: Nonparametric texture models became the dominant approach to texture modeling after 2000. They remained the primary method until generative models using neural networks emerged around 2014.
concepts.motivation_md: Nonparametric models were developed to overcome the limitations of fixed-parameter models by using the data itself to represent the texture.
concepts.recap_md:
- Became the dominant texture modeling approach after 2000.
- Preceded the rise of neural network generative models in 2014.

concepts.title: Nonparametric Markov Random Field Image Models

position.section_title: Efros-Leung Texture Analysis and Synthesis Model

concepts.one_liner: Nonparametric Markov random field image models define a pixel's probability distribution based on its surrounding neighborhood.
concepts.content: Nonparametric Markov random field image models define the probability distribution of a pixel as dependent on the neighborhood around that pixel. If the values of enough pixels surrounding a given pixel are specified, then the probability distribution of the given pixel is independent of the other pixels in the image. This image model can be used as a powerful texture synthesis model.
concepts.motivation_md: By assuming that local neighborhoods contain all the information necessary to predict a pixel, these models simplify the complex task of modeling global image statistics.
concepts.recap_md:
- Pixel probability depends only on its local neighborhood.
- Provides a powerful framework for texture synthesis.
- Assumes conditional independence from distant pixels given enough local context.

concepts.title: Efros-Leung Texture Analysis and Synthesis Model

position.section_title: Efros-Leung Texture Analysis and Synthesis Model

concepts.one_liner: The Efros-Leung algorithm is an iterative texture synthesis method that grows new textures by matching local neighborhoods from an input example.
concepts.content:
As with other texture synthesis algorithms, the input to the Efros-Leung algorithm is an example of the texture to be synthesized, and the output is an image of more of that texture. It is an iterative algorithm as shown in (see figure: In the Efros-Leung algorithm @Efros99).

At each iteration, we have synthesized pixels in the neighborhood of the pixel to be synthesized. We look through the input image for examples of similar configurations of pixel values as the current local neighborhood, having a sum of squared intensity differences from the local neighborhood lower than some threshold. Randomly select one of the matching instances, and copy the value of the pixel into the pixel to be synthesized. Repeat for all pixels to be synthesized. It can be natural to synthesize the pixels in a raster-scan ordering. Image pixels without sufficient neighboring pixels for context can be randomly sampled from the input texture.

In this nonparametric model, the representation of a texture is the reference image itself. There is not a low-dimensional representation as is the case with parametric texture models. The advantage is that no information is lost in this representation.









Synthesized texture from the Efros-Leung algorithm as a function of size of the context region. A very small context region only covers parts of features (like circles) and fails to complete them, while larger regions maintain individual features, and even larger regions enforce all spatial regularities of the input texture.

(see figure: Image synthesis results from the Efros-Leung algorithm. The small crops are used to synthesize the larger texture regions. Input images are 128 $\times$ 128 pixels, and the outputs are 256 $\times$...) 

While the model works remarkably well, artifacts like oversized features can occur. Increasing the neighborhood size can remove those issues, while decreasing it can help remove unwanted repetitions of reference elements.
concepts.motivation_md: This algorithm solves the problem of generating large, realistic texture regions from a small sample without needing a complex mathematical model of the texture's parameters.
concepts.recap_md:
- Synthesizes textures iteratively by matching local pixel neighborhoods to an input sample.
- Uses the reference image itself as the texture representation (nonparametric).
- Results depend heavily on the size of the context region used for matching.

concepts.title: Autoregressive Model
concepts.one_liner: An autoregressive model is a class of models, including the Efros-Leung algorithm, that predicts future values based on past values in a sequence.
concepts.content: The Efros-Leung algorithm is an autoregressive model. This class of models can be used in conjunction with deep networks to model data sequences or images by predicting the next element based on previous ones.
concepts.motivation_md: Autoregressive models provide a structured way to generate data sequentially, ensuring that each new piece of data is consistent with what has already been generated.
concepts.recap_md:
- Predicts the next value in a sequence based on previous values.
- The Efros-Leung algorithm serves as a classic example of this model type.

concepts.title: Diffusion Models
concepts.one_liner: Diffusion models are generative models that use an iterative denoising process to transform noise into structured images.
concepts.content: Diffusion models follow a strategy where an iterative process, similar to the denoising in the Heeger-Bergen algorithm, starts with a noise image and gradually transforms it into a structured image, such as a texture.
concepts.motivation_md: Diffusion models allow for the generation of high-quality, complex data by breaking the generation process into many small, manageable denoising steps.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses an iterative denoising process to generate images.
- Starts with random noise and transforms it into a structured output.

concepts.title: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
concepts.one_liner: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are models that learn to generate images matching the statistics of a set of exemplars using a discriminator network.
concepts.content: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) create images that have the same statistics as a set of exemplars. Unlike earlier methods like the Heeger-Bergen algorithm which use hand-defined subband statistics, GANs use a learned discriminator neural network to determine the statistics that need to be matched.
concepts.motivation_md: GANs automate the discovery of relevant features and statistics in data, allowing for the generation of highly realistic images without manual feature engineering.
concepts.recap_md:
- Generates images by matching the statistics of exemplar sets.
- Uses a discriminator neural network to learn which statistics to match.
- Contrast with hand-defined statistical methods like Heeger-Bergen.

key_passage.text: A GAN also makes images that have the same statistics as a set of exemplars; however, the statistics we seek to match are learned (by a so-called discriminator neural net) rather than hand-defined to be subband statistics.

concepts.title: Texture
concepts.one_liner: A texture is an image composed of a set of similar looking elements where the representation focuses on statistics rather than individual elements.
concepts.content: Texture is a concept intimately related to human perception. A texture is a type of image that is composed by a set of similar looking elements. A texture representation contains information about the statistics of its constituent elements, but not about the elements individually.
concepts.motivation_md: In many visual scenes, individual details (like blades of grass) are less important than the overall pattern. Defining texture allows us to model these patterns statistically.
concepts.recap_md: - Textures consist of repeating or similar visual elements.

concepts.title: Infinite texture generation algorithm
concepts.one_liner: Infinite texture generation can be achieved by cropping pieces from a large sample image, though this provides little insight into human perception.
concepts.content: Texture synthesis can be solved by a trivial algorithm: if we had access to a very large image of the texture we want to generate, we could just crop pieces from it to create new images. This is illustrated in (see figure: The infinite texture generation algorithm. If we had access to a very large image of the texture we want to generate, we could just crop pieces from it to create new images.). However, such an algorithm, although successful in practice, gives little understanding of how human perception works or how to modify textures to create new ones. It also does not help in determining which representations are useful for measuring similarity between textures.
concepts.motivation_md: While simple cropping works for basic synthesis, it doesn't help us understand the underlying mathematical or perceptual structure of textures, which is necessary for more complex editing or recognition tasks.
concepts.recap_md: - Simple cropping from a large sample can synthesize new texture instances.

concepts.title: Perception of sets

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Human vision processes small numbers of objects individually but represents larger groups as a single set.
concepts.content:
When an image is composed of one or a few distinct objects, we can easily pay attention to each of them individually and count them in parallel. For displays with one to four elements, the time it takes to report the number of elements does not depend on the count. However, when there are more than four or five objects, we seem to pay attention only to a few and represent the rest as a set. The perception of sets is an important area of study in human visual psychophysics.

(see figure: When looking at these images, we can count the number of circles at a glance if there are less than five circles. When an image has more than five items, we have to count them one by one.)
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how the brain transitions from individual object recognition to ensemble (set) perception helps explain how we process complex scenes and textures.
concepts.recap_md: - Small groups (up to 4) are processed in parallel and counted instantly.

concepts.title: Subitizing

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Subitizing is the ability to instantly determine the number of objects in a display without counting, effective for fewer than five elements.
concepts.content: The ability to know how many objects are in a display without counting them is called subitizing. This phenomenon only works when there are fewer than five elements in a display.
concepts.motivation_md: Subitizing reveals a specific limit in human pre-attentive processing, distinguishing between immediate numerical recognition and the serial process of counting.
concepts.recap_md: - Subitizing is the instant recognition of quantity without serial counting.

concepts.title: Crowding

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Crowding is a visual phenomenon where objects in peripheral vision become difficult to recognize when surrounded by other similar features.
concepts.content: Crowding is a visual phenomenon where features of objects in the periphery get entangled, making individual recognition difficult. This is illustrated in (see figure: Crowding. If you look at the central cross, the letter R on the right can be recognized, however the letter B on the left is hard to read.). Even if two letters are at the same distance from fixation, a letter surrounded by others (like the B) is harder to read than an isolated one (like the R). This is not due to low resolution, but because the pooling window for image features is larger than the individual objects, causing features to mix. Anything inside these pooling regions will suffer from crowding effects, which are larger than what would be predicted by receptor spacing alone.
concepts.motivation_md: Crowding explains the limitations of peripheral vision and suggests that the brain pools features over large spatial areas in the periphery, which is relevant for understanding how we perceive textures and cluttered scenes.
concepts.recap_md: - Peripheral objects are harder to identify when surrounded by other objects.

key_passage.text: As the letter B is surrounded by other letters, the features of the three letters get entangled as if the pooling window for image features was larger than the three letters together.

motivation.text: The reason cannot be due to the low resolution of peripheral vision as both letters are at the same distance from the fixation location. The explanation of this phenomena is due to something called crowding.

concepts.title: Textons

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Textons are fundamental texture elements whose statistical relationships define the analysis of textures.
concepts.content: Bela Julesz proposed that textures are analyzed in terms of statistical relationships between fundamental texture elements that he called textons. Historically, his models were restricted to binary images formed by simple elements, and it generally required a human observer to identify what those fundamental units were. (see figure: Texture discrimination using textons.)
concepts.motivation_md: To understand how humans perceive and discriminate between different textures by identifying the basic building blocks of visual patterns.
concepts.recap_md: - Textons are the fundamental units or elements that make up a texture.

concepts.title: Pre-attentive texture discrimination

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Pre-attentive texture discrimination can be explained by filter banks, where features based on filter outputs enable texture-based image segmentation.
concepts.content: A texture representation based on filter banks was introduced by Bergen and Adelson, and by Malik and Perona. They demonstrated that filters are capable of explaining several results of pre-attentive texture discrimination. Furthermore, features derived from filter outputs can be utilized to perform texture-based image segmentation.
concepts.motivation_md: To explain how the human visual system distinguishes textures rapidly and automatically without focused attention, using computational filters.
concepts.recap_md: - Filter banks provide a computational model for how humans discriminate textures pre-attentively.

concepts.title: Texture synthesis
concepts.one_liner: Texture synthesis is the process of generating new random samples of a texture that match the appearance of a given reference texture.
concepts.content: Texture synthesis is the problem of building a process that, given a reference texture, outputs images with new random samples of the same texture. This procedure typically involves taking a reference texture, extracting a representation $\theta$, and using that representation to transform a random noise image into a new sample of the desired texture. Texture synthesis is important for computer graphics applications and for studying which texture representations are useful for visual recognition.
concepts.motivation_md: To create realistic, non-repeating patterns for computer graphics and to evaluate the effectiveness of texture representations in computer vision.
concepts.recap_md: - The goal is to produce new images that look like random samples of a provided reference texture.

motivation.text: Texture synthesis is important for many computer graphics applications, and also as way of studying what representations of a texture can be useful for visual recognition.

concepts.title: Heeger-Bergen texture synthesis method
concepts.one_liner: The Heeger-Bergen method is a wavelet-based synthesis algorithm that characterizes texture by the probability distributions of various filter responses.
concepts.content: The Heeger-Bergen texture synthesis method is an influential wavelet-based algorithm published in 1995. The method is based on the conjecture that if two textures produce the same distribution of filter responses for all filters, they will look identical to a human observer. To implement this, the method uses a steerable pyramid to determine the full probability distribution of responses for filters applied at different scales and orientations.
concepts.motivation_md: To test the hypothesis that matching the histograms of filter responses across different scales and orientations is sufficient to replicate a texture's appearance.
concepts.recap_md: - It characterizes textures using the probability distributions (histograms) of filter responses.

key_passage.text: Bergen highlighted the value of measuring the mean-squared responses of filters applied to images for characterizing texture. He suggested that determining the full probability distribution of each filter's responses would be even more effective. He conjectured that if two textures produced the same distribution of filter responses for all filters, they would look identical to a human observer.

concepts.title: Texture analysis
concepts.one_liner: Texture analysis is the process of extracting a representation, $\theta$, from a reference texture.
concepts.content: Texture analysis of a reference texture extracts a texture representation, $\theta$. This representation captures the essential characteristics of the texture and is used as a parameter for subsequent synthesis or recognition tasks.
concepts.motivation_md: To capture the essential mathematical or statistical characteristics of a texture so it can be reconstructed or recognized.
concepts.recap_md: - Analysis involves extracting a set of parameters or a representation, $\theta$, from an input texture.

slots.example: Texture analysis of a reference texture extracts a texture representation, $\theta$. This representation captures the essential characteristics of the texture and is used as a parameter for subsequent synthesis or recognition tasks.

concepts.title: Heeger-Bergen texture synthesis algorithm
concepts.one_liner: The Heeger-Bergen algorithm iteratively matches the histograms of an image and its filter subbands to synthesize a texture from noise.
concepts.content: The Heeger-Bergen texture synthesis algorithm is an iterative procedure that begins with a random noise image and uses parameters $\theta$ to produce an improved image. (see figure: The steps of the Heeger-Bergen texture synthesis algorithm. The process starts with white noise input image. Each step takes as input the previous output, and it is modified by a function...) First, a reference texture is decomposed into multiple orientations and scales using oriented filters, such as a steerable pyramid. The final texture representation is the concatenation of the histograms from all subbands, the low-pass residual, and the input image. (see figure: (a) Texture analysis (encoder) using a steerable pyramid with six orientations and three scales. The output representation is the concatenation of the 18 subband histograms, the low-pass residual...) The crux of the algorithm is to alternate between matching the intensity domain pixel histogram of the image and matching the histograms of the transform domain subbands. Histogram matching is implemented by a pointwise monotonic nonlinearity. (see figure: Histogram matching for one of the subbands. The same operation is done for all the subbands independently.) After several iterations of these matching steps in both domains, the algorithm converges to the synthesized texture.
concepts.motivation_md: To provide a concrete computational method for synthesizing textures by enforcing statistical consistency across multiple scales and orientations.
concepts.recap_md: - It starts with white noise and iteratively refines it to match the target texture's statistics.

key_passage.text: The crux of the algorithm is to alternate matching the intensity domain pixel histogram of the image, then to transform the resulting image into the transform domain and enforce a match, subband by subband, of the image histograms there.

motivation.text: First, the reference texture is decomposed multiple orientation and scales as the outputs of many oriented filters over different spatial scales. The transform should represent all spatial frequencies of the image, so that all aspects of a texture can be synthesized, and the subbands should not be aliased, to avoid artifacts in the synthesized results.

concepts.title: Histogram matching
concepts.one_liner: Histogram matching is a technique that uses a pointwise monotonic nonlinearity to modify an image's pixel or subband values to match a target distribution.
concepts.content: Histogram matching is implemented by a pointwise monotonic nonlinearity. (see figure: Histogram matching for one of the subbands. The same operation is done for all the subbands independently.) In the context of texture synthesis, the histogram of a reference texture subband often has a Laplacian shape, while the initial noise subband has a Gaussian distribution. Histogram matching modifies the values of each subband pixel based on the current and target pixel histograms. This process can make the noise subband look sparser, setting many values to zero to match the target distribution. The same operation is performed for all subbands in a steerable pyramid.
concepts.motivation_md: To force one image to have the same first-order statistics (pixel value distribution) as another, which is a key step in matching texture appearance.
concepts.recap_md: - It uses a pixelwise nonlinearity to transform one probability distribution into another.

key_passage.text: Histogram matching is implemented by a pointwise monotonic nonlinearity.

motivation.text: Histogram matching modifies the values of each subband pixel (the histogram matching function is a pixelwise nonlinearity that depends on the current and target pixel histograms). After histogram matching, the noise subband looks sparser, with many values set to zero.

concepts.title: Heeger-Bergen limitations and results
concepts.one_liner: While effective for many textures, the Heeger-Bergen algorithm fails to capture correlations across scales and struggles with large-scale structures.
concepts.content: The Heeger-Bergen algorithm often produces good results for textures like simple geometric patterns. However, it does not capture correlations of filter responses across different scales, which means long or large-scale structures are often depicted poorly. (see figure: Two examples of synthesized textures. Inputs have a size of 256 $\times$ 256 pixels, outputs are 512 $\times$ 512. In these examples, the algorithm runs for 15 iterations, using a pyramid of six...) To process color images, principal component analysis (PCA) is first used to find decorrelated color components, and then texture analysis-synthesis is applied to each channel independently. The final image is produced by projecting back into the original color space. Notably, the algorithm is typically run for a limited number of iterations (e.g., 15), as adding more iterations can make the images look worse.
concepts.motivation_md: To identify the strengths and weaknesses of the Heeger-Bergen approach, particularly its inability to model higher-order dependencies between different scales.
concepts.recap_md: - The method struggles with large-scale structures because it ignores correlations between different pyramid scales.

key_passage.text: However, we note that correlations of filter responses across scale is not captured in this procedure, and long or large-scale structures are often depicted poorly.

prereq.rationale: This algorithm is a specific (though trivial) method for synthesizing the 'texture' defined in this section.
Nonparametric texture models are a specific class of models developed for the purpose of texture modeling and synthesis.
The Efros-Leung algorithm is a concrete implementation of the nonparametric Markov random field image model.
The algorithm is a specific iterative technique used to perform texture synthesis from an input example.
Texture synthesis is defined as the process of generating new samples of a specific reference texture.
The Heeger-Bergen method is a specific, influential algorithm designed to solve the texture synthesis problem.
Texture analysis is the prerequisite step of extracting a representation from a given reference texture.
The algorithm is the specific iterative implementation of the conceptual Heeger-Bergen method.
The algorithm begins by performing texture analysis on a reference image to create a target representation.
In this context, histogram matching is the specific mechanism used to modify noise subbands to match the reference texture's characteristics.
The limitations and results discussed are direct evaluations of the Heeger-Bergen algorithm's performance.
Parametric models rely on texture analysis to extract the small vector of parameters that represent the image.
Textons are proposed as the fundamental units for analyzing textures.

overlay.rationale: Nonparametric models represent a shift in methodology from the earlier parametric models that dominated texture research before 2000.
Nonparametric MRFs are a specific type of nonparametric model used for texture synthesis.
Analysis and synthesis are complementary halves of the texture generation process.
Parametric texture models are the broader class of models that include the Heeger-Bergen method.
Subitizing is the specific case of set perception that occurs when there are fewer than five elements.
Crowding is often interpreted as a transition from individual object recognition to texture-like pooling of features.
Filter-based models are an alternative or evolution of Julesz's earlier texton-based theory of texture discrimination.
The Efros-Leung algorithm is a specific instance of the autoregressive model class, which predicts future values from past ones.
The iterative denoising process in diffusion models is compared to the approach used in the Heeger-Bergen algorithm.
GANs are contrasted with the Heeger-Bergen algorithm, as they learn statistics via a discriminator rather than using hand-defined ones.
